data.alt_text: A simple cartoon diagram of the Earth's tilt in relation to the rays from the Sun shows 3 places in the Earth's orbit representing different seasons. Slim white handwritten text reads, "What Causes the Seasons?"
data.grid_description: Many people believe that Earth is closer to the Sun in the summer and that is why it is hotter. And, likewise, they think Earth is farthest from the Sun in the winter. Although this idea makes sense, it is incorrect! Click to learn what really causes the seasons on Earth.

data.grid_title: Explore Black Holes with Multiple Senses
data.alt_text: An artist's depiction of a black hole shows a dark sphere engulfed in a swirling brown disk of material and a beam of neon purple- light emitting from the black spere at the center. Thin white text reads, "Explore Black Holes with Multiple Senses."
data.grid_description: A trio of NASA telescopes, in conjunction with others on the ground, is helping astronomers learn more about the Milky Way's supermassive black hole. These data will help astronomers better understand the complex process of "accretion" where material falls towards and into the black hole. Click to learn more about how NASA explores black holes.

data.grid_title: CubeSat Builder: Build a NASA Spacecraft!
data.alt_text: A pixelated character from the CubeSat Builder game is running across a laboratory holding a blue and yellow box while sweating from their effort. Bold yellow text on a royal blue background reads, "CubeSat Builder: Build a NASA Spacecraft. How many CubeSats can you assemble?"
data.grid_description: In the NASA game CubeSat Builder, build as many CubeSat spacecraft as possible in a NASA cleanroom before time runs out! Like a chef preparing food for hungry customers, build CubeSats for engineers according to the project blueprints they send in. Run around the clean room, test CubeSat parts, assemble CubeSats, and perform final tests before sending them off to the launch pad. Juggle the testing of parts while assembling more than one CubeSat at a time to build them faster!

data.grid_title: Create Your Own Paper Airplane Version of NASA's X-59!
data.alt_text: The X-59 aircraft flies high about the Earth's surface and wispy clouds can be seen below. The airplane itself is long, narrow, and white in color with a pointy nose segment.
data.grid_description: The X-59(is one of NASA’s newest experimental aircraft and it is designed to lower the noise created by planes flying faster than the speed of sound. When planes fly supersonic (faster than the speed of sound), the pressure waves they create combine together and produce a very loud noise called a sonic boom. This noise is so loud that it can damage property and disturb animals. Grab a piece of paper, some tape, and a pair of scissors to make your own X-59 at home today!

data.grid_title: Make a Fan Representing Earth's Layers!
data.alt_text: A fully lit image of Earth sits on a pitch black- background. On the Earth, swirling clouds drape over large blue oceans and patchy green land masses. Above Earth, bold white text reads, "Make a Fan Representing Earth's Layers!"
data.grid_description: We spend pretty much all our time on Earth’s crust. It’s where all the land and oceans are. But below the crust, there’s a lot going on. To remember that Earth is much more than just the surface we see every day, make this Earth layer fan!

data.grid_title: Build a Coding Antenna with NASA!
data.alt_text: Against a black background, small green numbers and letters trickle down the image giving it a computer data feel. Over that, bold text reads, "Build your own coding antenna. Create secret messages for your family and friends."
data.grid_description: Practice your engineering skills by decorating and assembling your own ground station antenna, then use it as a wheel cipher to help NASA decode three secret messages. Ciphers have been used for thousands of years to help keep information hidden. After cracking NASA’s code, use your antenna cipher to create your own secret messages for your friends and family!

data.grid_description: This open source code app provides the capability to interactively browse over 1000 global, full-resolution satellite imagery layers and then download the underlying data. Many of the imagery layers are updated daily and are available within three hours of observation - essentially showing the entire Earth as it looks "right now".

data.alt_text: Astronaut Nicole Mann holds a plastic straw with a small bubble of water sitting on top. Bold white text reads, "Bring space into your classroom. Quick tutorials from astronauts in space accompanied by lesson plans."
data.grid_description: Ever wonder what it is about water that makes it so important for life? In this STEMonstration, NASA astronaut Nicole Mann demonstrates the role water’s solvent properties play aboard the space station and explains what makes water so important for life as we know it. Explore the six properties of water that distinguish it from other liquids and check out the corresponding classroom connection to determine how water’s molecular structure relates to its unique properties.
